value.overview: The Black-capped Antthrush (Formicarius nigricapillus) is a secretive, ground-dwelling antthrush of humid mountain forests in southern Central America. It spends most of its time walking quietly through leaf litter, where it searches for small invertebrates. The species was formerly treated as part of the broader Black-headed Antthrush complex, but the Costa Rican and Panamanian form is now recognized as a separate species. Costa Rica is an important part of its limited range.
value.classification: The Black-capped Antthrush belongs to the order Passeriformes and family Formicariidae. Its scientific name is Formicarius nigricapillus, and it is currently treated as a monotypic species following the separation of the former Chocó population as the Black-hooded Antthrush, Formicarius destructus.
value.identification: This medium-sized antthrush is approximately 18 cm long. Adults have a dark brown body, a blackish cap, and black facial and throat areas, with a conspicuous bluish-white area of bare skin around the eye. The underparts are generally dark and subdued, while the back and wings are brown. It is usually detected by its deliberate walk, upright posture, and distinctive ringing or trilling song rather than by prolonged views.
value.rangeHabitat: The Black-capped Antthrush occurs in Costa Rica and Panama, mainly in humid forests on the Caribbean slope and in suitable forest on both slopes of Panama. In Costa Rica, it is locally common but occupies a narrow elevational belt: roughly 400–800 m in the north and central regions, and about 600–1,200 m in the southeast. It favors primary wet forest and may occasionally enter adjacent mature secondary growth. It is replaced by related antthrushes at lower or higher elevations.
value.migrationStatus: It is considered a year-round resident, including in Costa Rica. No regular seasonal migration is known; individuals generally remain in suitable forest habitat throughout the year.
value.breeding: In Costa Rica, breeding has been reported mainly in April and May. A documented nest was a shallow cup made from leaf petioles and dry leaves, placed inside a hollow palm stump. The clutch consists of two eggs, which are described as dull white and soon becoming marked with brown. Information on incubation, nestling development, and parental care remains limited.
value.dietFeeding: The species feeds mainly on arthropods, especially insects and spiders, and may also take very small reptiles and amphibians. It forages almost entirely on or close to the ground, walking slowly through leaf litter and probing crevices, tangles, and fallen vegetation. It may flick aside leaves to expose prey and can sometimes follow army-ant swarms to capture animals fleeing the advancing ants.
value.behavior: Black-capped Antthrushes are shy, difficult-to-see forest birds that usually occur alone or in pairs. They move deliberately along the forest floor, often holding the tail cocked and pausing frequently while searching for prey. Both sexes may sing, commonly from low perches or near the ground. Their songs and calls are more often heard than the birds are seen, especially in dense, wet understory.

conservation.populationTrend: The population trend of the separately recognized Black-capped Antthrush is not well established. The species is locally common in parts of its range and occurs in protected forests, but it is uncommon in Costa Rica and has a geographically limited distribution.
